primitives.verbatim_quote: In this case a judicious use of long high punts of a twisting variety, well followed up by the forwards, will often result in securing touch-downs, or repeated long gains, from their muffing.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'K': 'kick type index (dimensionless)', 'M': 'muff probability (dimensionless)', 'G': 'gain per muff (yards)', 'F': 'follow-up efficiency (dimensionless)'}

The first primitive identifies that excessive play disguise leads to inefficiency through fatigue, modeled as a trade-off between play complexity (P) and team endurance (T). The second primitive leverages opponent weakness—specifically poor catching—to derive a probabilistic gain function (G) dependent on muff probability (M) and follow-up execution (F). The third primitive formalizes the concept of exploiting a known weakness (W) over time, where cumulative fatigue (C) acts as a limiting factor against repetitive assault rate (R) and attack efficacy (A). These primitives form a layered decision framework where each layer introduces a constraint or opportunity, enabling a dual perspective: optimizing immediate gains while managing long-term resource depletion. The interplay between these primitives reflects a game-theoretic equilibrium where strategic surprise and sustained pressure coexist.
